newsitem.title: USA: Motorola sees Japan deal revs in Q4 1997.
newsitem.headline: Motorola sees Japan deal revs in Q4 1997.

text.p: Motorola Inc said Wednesday revenues from its contract with two Japanese wireless phone operators will begin to trickle in during the fourth quarter of 1997, adding the deal is an important step for both the company and its cellular technology.

"We expect the bulk of the revenue to be recognized in 1998 and after, with maybe a little in the fourth quarter of 1997," Jack Scanlon, president and general manager of Motorola Cellular Networks and Space Sector, said in a conference call.
Shares of Motorola traded 3-1/4 higher at 61-5/8.

Motorola landed a lucrative contract with DDI Corp and IDO Corp, an affiliate of Toyota Motor Corp, which will spend 300 billion yen or nearly $3 billion to jointly introduce a new digital cell phone service in Japan beginning in April 1998.
Motorola will provide code division multiple access (CDMA) infrastructure for the companies.
Although the value of the contract was not disclosed, the company said it will include installation of more than 1,500 base stations at a price of $500,000 to $1 million each.
Rakesh Sood, an analyst for Hambrecht & Quist, said he estimates Motorola will receive at least half of the $3 billion to be invested in the network expansion.
Analysts also agreed that, for Motorola, this could lead to other contracts in Japan as well.
"Certainly as they (IDO and DDO) announce the handset (cell phone) orders I would expect Motorola to have a good opportunity there too," Sood said.
"It's definitely a bullish sign," Monish Bahl, an analyst for Parker/Hunter Inc, added. "I think it's another step for Motorola and CDMA technology."
Japan was the fastest growing cellular market last year and is the second largest worldwide, Motorola said. The cellular penetration rate is just 13 percent, the company said.
Motorola said it among others is also working with Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp of Japan to develop the specifications for a future CDMA technology for a project scheduled after the year 2000.
"If you read between the lines you would expect they would get some kind of an award from them at some point," Sood said.

Motorola has invested heavily in CDMA, and Scanlon called the contract a "tremendous endorsement" of the technology. Motorola's archrivals Telefon AB L.M. Ericsson of Sweden and Nokia Oy of Finland are not big players in CDMA, but focus more on competing technology.
Motorola said the technology to be used in Japan is its new enhanced CDMA, which will allow the companies to increase the network capacity to at least 20 million subscribers from about two million.
Scanlon said international contracts are increasingly more important to Motorola as cellular markets outside the United States and Europe are growing about twice as fast.
